facts.claim: Chapter 'Lesson 4: The History of Taxes and the Power of Corporations' opens with Robin Hood: Kiyosaki's teacher called him a romantic hero; rich dad called Robin Hood a crook.

Rich dad's tax history as told in the book: temporary war taxes (Britain against Napoleon 1799-1816, America for the Civil War 1861-1865); England made income tax permanent in 1874; the US in 1913 with the 16th Amendment; taxes were first levied only on the rich, then spread to the middle class and the poor.
Book's core contrast: 'Employees earn and get taxed, and they try to live on what is left. A corporation earns, spends everything it can, and is taxed on anything that is left.'
facts.source: Book text, section on Financial IQ / Tax advantages

facts.claim: Kiyosaki describes a corporation as 'merely a file folder with some legal documents in it' sitting in an attorney's office, registered with a state agency.
The book's examples of corporate expenses: vacations as 'board meetings in Hawaii', car payments, insurance, repairs, health-club memberships; he calls it legal and done with pre-tax dollars.
Kiyosaki writes that average Americans work four to five months a year for the government just to cover taxes ('working from January to May').
When young Robert told rich dad his father's advice to climb the corporate ladder, rich dad chuckled: 'Why not own the ladder?'

Rich dad paid for smart tax accountants and attorneys because it was cheaper than paying the government; his line: 'Be smart and you won't be pushed around as much.' Financial IQ in the book has four parts: accounting, investing, understanding markets, the law.

Critics (Motley Fool, John T. Reed, Finmasters) call the corporate tax advice oversimplified at best; deducting personal vacations or gym dues through a company can be illegal. The existence of a real 'rich dad' is also disputed.
facts.source: Motley Fool; johntreed.com; Finmasters; White Coat Investor

facts.claim: Book: the rich created the corporation in the days of sailing ships to limit risk to the money invested in each voyage; if the ship was lost the crew lost their lives, the investors only the money put into that voyage.
Rich dad reminded Mike and Robert that the biggest bully was not the boss or the supervisor but the tax man, who will always take more if you let him.

rejected.claim: Employee: earn -> pay tax -> spend; owner: earn -> spend (business costs) -> pay tax, presented as plain fact without caveat
rejected.reason: The order is in the book, but whether personal costs are deductible depends on law; kept only as Kiyosaki's claim with an editorial caveat

rejected.claim: 'The wealth gap between the two approaches becomes huge over decades'
rejected.reason: No such figure or statement verified in the book

rejected.claim: People spend on homes, cars, education but invest nothing in financial literacy, as 'Kiyosaki's biggest complaint'
'Financial literacy is not a luxury' as a quoted line
rejected.reason: Not in the book as a quote

1293.note: Center (earn-spend-tax order) is in Lesson 4. Rebuilt around Robin Hood, tax history, the file-folder corporation and the 'own the ladder' line, with an editorial caveat on legality.
